newsitem.title: USA: FAA moves to charge planes for U.S. airspace use. [CORRECTED 23:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FAA moves to charge planes for U.S. airspace use. [CORRECTED 23:40 GMT]

text.p: The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday that it submitted for public comment an interim final rule that will begin charging user fees to aircraft flying through U.S. airspace but which do not take off or land in the United States.
Currently, overflights that do not land or take off in the United States make no payments for aviation services provided to them by the FAA.
The FAA said the rule, which will be implentend on May 19, is consistent with international practices and is expected to recover about $90 million in fee revenue for fiscal year 1998.
FAA was given authority to charge fees to aircraft conducting U.S. overflights in the Federal Aviation Reauthorization Act of 1996.

The interim final rule will be published March 20 in the Federal Register, 60 days prior to the May 19 implementation date. FAA will conduct a meeting for public comment on May 1, and said that it is accepting comments over the next 120 days.
FAA said it will then issue a final rule after thorough review of the comments.

"This rule assesses a fair fee to aircraft operating in the safest air traffic control system in the world," Acting FAA Administrator Barry Valentine said. "The charging of overflight fees is consistent with most nations' practices, and will recover most of the cost of services from overflights."

The rule bases its overflight fees on distance flown through U.S.-controlled airspace. Fees are directly related to the cost of overflight services, and apply only to aircraft that neither take off from nor land in the United States.
The rule does not apply to aircraft owned by the United States or foreign governments.

Fees are assessed for flights through U.S. airspace, as well as flights through international airspace for which International Civil Aviation Organization has given the United States air traffic control responsibility.
The fees are applied in a "Tiered Charging System." General aviation piston-powered aircraft are charged no fees for overflight operations under 250 nautical miles.

In addition, Canada-to-Canada overflights in the United States have been granted deferral of the fees until October 1. The delay will give Canada time to institute its planned domestic enroute charge system, minimizing temporary disruption of air traffic due to introduction of the charges.
